item.title: Armored Likho BusySnake Campaign, Pegasus Hacks, and QR Code Quishing
item.content:encoded:
Armored Likho digging a snake pit: inside the covert BusySnake Stealer campaign — Must Read

Kaspersky uncovered an active Armored Likho phishing campaign targeting government and electric power organizations in Russia, Brazil, and Kazakhstan with a new Python infostealer called BusySnake Stealer. The malware uses AI-generated loaders, PyArmor obfuscation, browser credential and cookie theft, persistence via scheduled tasks, and built-in reverse SSH tunneling for stealthy access and data exfiltration.

  • Kaspersky uncovered an active phishing campaign tied to the previously unknown APT group Armored Likho, also known as Eagle Werewolf based on circumstantial evidence, targeting government agencies and the electric power sector in Russia, Brazil, and Kazakhstan.
  • The campaign uses malicious archive attachments containing EXE droppers or LNK files, including LNK files that abuse ZDI-CAN-25373 to hide command-line content and execute PowerShell-based downloaders.
  • The primary payload is BusySnake Stealer, a previously undocumented Python-based infostealer protected with PyArmor Pro 9.2.0 and designed to run on Windows without opening a console window.
  • BusySnake Stealer can steal clipboard data, documents, screenshots, browser passwords, browser cookies, 2FA secrets, cryptocurrency wallet JSON files, and Telegram session data, and it can establish reverse SSH tunnels and interact with RustDesk for remote control.
  • A newer BusySnake Stealer version creates scheduled tasks through the Windows Schedule.Service COM object, adds delayed execution to bypass dynamic analysis, and introduces a task-management framework for commands and in-memory execution of Python scripts from the C2 server.

European Parliament Member Investigating Spyware Was Hacked With Pegasus — Should Read

Citizen Lab found that former European Parliament member Stelios Kouloglou was repeatedly hacked with NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware while serving on the EU committee investigating spyware abuse. The infections may have exposed confidential committee work and suggest a Pegasus customer authorized to operate across multiple European countries was behind the targeting.

  • Citizen Lab reported that former Member of the European Parliament Stelios Kouloglou had his mobile device repeatedly hacked with Pegasus spyware while serving on the European Parliament committee investigating the use of Pegasus and similar surveillance tools.
  • Citizen Lab’s forensic analysis found that Kouloglou’s iPhone was compromised on or around October 21, 2022, and again on March 6 and 7, 2023, while the device was running iOS 15.5.
  • Researchers assessed that the attacks used a zero-click exploit in Apple’s HomeKit smart home software, codenamed PWNYOURHOME, which Apple addressed in iOS 16.3.1.
  • Citizen Lab said the infections have not been attributed to a specific government and that there is no evidence the Greek government was behind the activity.
  • The report said the first infection overlapped with a prior campaign targeting Russian and Belarusian-speaking exiled journalists and activists in Europe through the same email address, suggesting a Pegasus customer authorized to spy in multiple European countries may have been responsible.

The Payroll Memo Whose Link You Could Not Scan: QR Code Quishing Buried in a Word Attachment — Should Read

A payroll-themed phishing email used a Word attachment containing only a QR-code image that led to a credential-harvesting site, bypassing normal email URL scanning and pushing the victim to use a phone outside corporate protections. The key lesson is that defenses must inspect attachments, decode embedded QR codes, and correlate context like failed authentication and self-addressed sender patterns.

  • A procurement employee received a blank email containing a Word document named Revised_Pay_Structure_Notice.docx that appeared to be a personalized HR salary memo.
  • The only payload in the document was an embedded QR code image that decoded to a credential-harvesting URL on the domain weststrionvde[.]vu.
  • The malicious destination was not inspected by inline URL scanners because the link was encoded in pixels inside an image nested in an Office document rather than appearing as text in the email body.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all failed, and the sender address was the recipient’s own address.
  • The attachment was a 43,915-byte DOCX with no macros, and the article says detection requires reading inside documents, decoding embedded QR codes, and evaluating the resulting destination.

The Silent Push Difference — Optional

Silent Push promotes its platform as a proactive threat intelligence solution that scans global internet infrastructure daily to identify attacker infrastructure before it is used. Its key claim is that “Indicators of Future Attack” help security teams block threats before attacks are launched.

  • Silent Push says the global security industry tracks only 2% of live attacker infrastructure and that it focuses on the remaining 98%.
  • Silent Push states that its mission is to neutralize attacker infrastructure before it becomes a threat by shifting cybersecurity from reactive responses to proactive, data-driven threat hunting.
  • Silent Push says traditional threat intelligence relies on stale Indicators of Compromise, which are post-breach artifacts showing where an attack has already been.
  • Silent Push says it scans the entire global IPv4 and IPv6 space daily to create a first-party database of internet-facing infrastructure without relying on third-party aggregators.
  • Silent Push says it creates Indicators of Future Attack by analyzing how adversaries build and manage infrastructure to identify proactive domains, IPs, and DNS records before an attack is launched.

What is Traffic Origin? — Optional

Silent Push is promoting Traffic Origin, a tool that aims to reveal the true upstream source controlling network connections so organizations can proactively block or challenge suspicious traffic before infrastructure is weaponized.

  • Traditional security stacks are described as reactive because they identify malicious infrastructure only after it has been weaponized.
  • Silent Push Traffic Origin is presented as a way to shift security from reactive investigation to proactive validation.
  • Traffic Origin aims to unmask the true upstream source of a connection rather than relying on simple IP geolocation.
  • The article says Traffic Origin helps organizations reach a state of “Origin Certainty.”
  • The article says Traffic Origin is built to detect upstream control signals that are invisible to traditional intelligence.
